section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that just as the Ten Utterances in action have a general utterance that includes all others, so too in their source in the Sefiros there are levels of general and particular, from Chochmah up through the will before the Tzimtzum.
section.t: And behold, just as it is with the Ten Utterances as they were drawn forth in action and revelation
(in the Sefirah of Malchus19),
that the utterance of Bereishis is a general utterance that includes all the utterances,
so too is it in their source,
in the Ten Sefiros,
that the utterance of Bereishis is the general principle,
and there are several levels to this20.
For in the Targum Yerushalmi it is stated: "Bereishis — with wisdom21,"
that Chochmah22
is the general principle that includes all the Sefiros.
And in Targum Onkelos it is stated: "Bereishis — in the beginning,"
and this refers to the will of Kesser that is above Chochmah22,
and even up to the primordial thought of Adam Kadmon, which is the general will for the entirety of Hishtalshelus,
and higher still, the will to create worlds as it is before the Tzimtzum,
which is a level of general principle also relative to the primordial thought of Adam Kadmon.
And within the Tzimtzum itself there is also general and particular,
for after it arose in His will, He envisioned within Himself, in potential, all that was destined to be in actuality,
for the will and the envisioning are levels of general and particular23.
And it is found,
that just as the drawing forth of Torah is in the manner of general and particular in many levels,
as above,
so too is it in the drawing forth of worlds, which is in the manner of general and particular in many levels.
And also in this one must understand,
behold, the intention in the creation of the worlds is that there should be particular creations with division,
and this intention is the cause for the arousal of the will before the Tzimtzum, in order that from it there should later be drawn forth
(through the multiplicity of Hishtalshelus)
ten particular utterances from which particular creations will come into being,

and if so, it would seemingly have been necessary for the arousal of the will to be from the outset in a particular manner, in a way that it would be possible for the coming into being of particular creations to come from it, in accordance with the intention,
and why was the arousal of the will initially in the manner of a general principle?

section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section uses the analogy of a teacher imparting wisdom to a student to explain why the initial influence must be in a concise, general manner, beginning as a point, to ensure proper limitation and alignment with the recipient.
section.t: And this will be understood through the analogy of the influence of intellect from a teacher to a student,
for our Sages said24,
"A person should always teach his student in a concise way,"
and it is known25
the precise meaning of the phrase "concise way"
(and not "a concise intellect"),
that he must influence the student with all the depth and details that are in the intellect,
except that all this must be taught to him in a concise way,
in brief words,
from which the student can understand all the details.
And like the Mishnah that our holy Rabbi taught us,
for in the language of the Mishnah there are
(in concealment)
all the details,
the length, breadth, and depth,
that are later explained in the Gemara,
except that in the Mishnah they are in extreme brevity26.
And the reason for this
(that the influence must specifically be in a concise way)
is,
because if he were to influence him
(at the outset)
with all the details in revelation,
the student's senses would become confused,
and also it is possible that due to the multiplicity of expansion it would go in a crooked path,
therefore he must specifically teach him in a concise way,
for through this the intellect comes in a limited form
(that he knows the matter in its generality),
and through this,
behold, even after he delves into the details,
with a multiplicity of reasoning,
the expansion will be according to the manner of the form of the concise words and will not go in a crooked path.
And just as it is in the actual influence to the student,
that the beginning of the influence must specifically be in a concise way,
so too is it in the invention of the intellect that pertains to the student within the teacher himself,
that the beginning of the drawing forth
(and invention)
of the intellect is in the manner of a point.
For behold, it is known27
that in the teacher's intellect is also included the externality of the intellect that pertains to the student,
except,
that when it is included in the teacher's intellect,
behold, in addition to it not being discernible there on its own
(because it is included and mixed with the internality),
behold, even the externality of the intellect
(that pertains to the student)
is in a multiplicity of light,
therefore the teacher must contract his intellect,
meaning to conceal his own essential intellect so that it does not shine at all,
for through this the externality becomes separated from the internality and is discernible on its own,
and also the externality that is found with him then is only in the manner of a point,
and only after this
(before he actually influences)
does he envision within himself the details that he will influence to the recipient.
And the reason for this, that initially the intellect comes in the manner of a point, is,
because if the intellect that pertains to the student were found from the outset in a manner of expansion with a multiplicity of details,
then the details would be in a manner as they flow from the teacher's intellect,
in a multiplicity of light,
and they would not be directed and suited to the student's senses.
Therefore,
the invention of the intellect initially is in the manner of a point
(a matter of concealment),
for through this the intellect becomes bounded.
For despite the fact that in the point are included all the details that he will later influence to the student
[and moreover,
that in the point there is also, in concealment, from the internality of the intellect28],
nevertheless,
since all this is in concealment,
behold, through this a boundary and form
(general)
is made in the intellect, so that it will be in a manner that is fit to be influenced to the student,
and after this boundary is made in it,
behold, even after it is drawn forth in breadth and expansion
(when he specifies the details),
the breadth will be according to the manner of the boundary and form of the point.

section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section applies the analogy above to the Divine realm, explaining that the initial drawing forth of light from Ein Sof had to be in a general manner to create a bounded form suitable for the worlds, so that subsequent details would also be within that measure.
section.t: And the analogue from this will be understood Above,
that in order for the light that brings worlds into being to be commensurate with the creatures,
in a way that it can shine within them internally,
it was necessary that there first be a drawing forth in the manner of general and particular.
For since the worlds are incomparable relative to the Ein Sof light,
therefore,
if the drawing forth from Ein Sof were from the outset in a multiplicity of details,
then the details would be without limit
(as they are from the perspective of Ein Sof),
therefore it was necessary that there first be a drawing forth in the manner of a general principle,
for through this a general form is made in the light, so that it will be commensurate with the worlds,
and through this,
even the details that are drawn forth afterward are according to this form.
